c.v: This stage makes every run produce something another engineer can act on. Until now a run left two files: a verdict, which says pass or fail and lists the checks, and a small environment file with the commit and a few versions. Neither of them says what was asked for, and nothing ties them together, so a failure sent to a colleague arrived as a paste with no context around it.

The decision worth defending is that the report names what it could not record. The reproducibility topic listed the facts two runs need before they can be compared, and the bench has only some of them: there is no container image yet, and no seed is passed to Gazebo. A report that quietly left those out would read as complete. So the list lives in
, every report prints a section naming what is absent, and the gap stays visible in each run until somebody closes it.
What we can now show: one Markdown file per run carrying its inputs, its environment, its timing on both clocks and its verdict, with the missing facts named at the bottom of every one.

subs.title: Run report with inputs, versions and results

c.v: By the end of this session,
can turn a verdict and a list of facts into a report, with GoogleTest tests you wrote first and saw fail, and a
tool that does it from the command line.

The reader of this file is a colleague who was not there, or you in three months, which is the same person. They arrive with a link and no context, and they need three questions answered before they can do anything: what was run, where it ran, and what happened. The verdict answers the third. The environment file answers a third of the second. Nothing at all answers the first, which is why a failing run currently has to be explained in a message rather than read.

There is a fourth question, and it is the one that separates a report from a dump. What about this run cannot be compared with another? The reproducibility topic was blunt about it: two runs are comparable when they come from the same container image and only approximately otherwise, and the bench has no image for scenario runs yet. A report that lists what it has and stops implies that what it has is enough. This one carries the checklist and prints what is missing from it, so the absence is on the page rather than in somebody's memory.

Add one case each for: a fact found in any of the three groups counts as present; a report whose verdict is empty says so in its title rather than crashing; the verdict's text appears in the report unchanged; and a record with every required fact prints no section about what is absent. Add
to watch it fail to compile.

c.v: Read the bottom of it first. Two facts are missing, and the report says which, so nobody reading this run has to work out whether it can be held against yesterday's. The image digest is missing because the bench has no image for scenario runs, which the CI topic builds. The seed is missing because nothing passes one to Gazebo yet, which is the next session's work. Neither is a surprise, and that is the point: a surprise is what you get when a report leaves a field out instead of printing it empty.

items.v: searches all three groups for a name, so moving a fact from one table to another cannot silently turn it into a missing one. A fact whose value is an empty string counts as absent rather than as present and blank, which is what the shell produces when a command it ran found nothing. And the verdict goes into the report verbatim, indented by four spaces rather than reformatted: the runner already decided how that text reads, and two formats for one fact is how they start disagreeing. The indent is there instead of a fence because a report is Markdown that other Markdown quotes, and a fence inside a fence ends the outer one early.

items.v: today from four commands; that file becomes the facts file, with the sections and every fact the report asks for:

blocks.text:
facts="results/$name.facts"
{ echo "[inputs]"
  echo "scenario: $name"
  echo "launch arguments: ${*:2}"
  echo "parameter file: $(sha256sum "install/bench_sim/share/bench_sim/config/$name.yaml" | cut -c1-16)"
  echo "seed: ${BENCH_SEED:-}"
  echo "[environment]"
  echo "commit: $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"
  echo "working tree: $(git status --porcelain | wc -l) files modified"
  echo "image digest: ${BENCH_IMAGE_DIGEST:-}"
  echo "os: $(lsb_release -ds)"
  echo "gazebo: $(gz sim --version | head -1)"
  echo "tb3 sim: $(dpkg-query -W ros-jazzy-nav2-minimal-tb3-sim)"
  echo "rmw: ${RMW_IMPLEMENTATION:-rmw_fastrtps_cpp default}"
  echo "domain id: ${ROS_DOMAIN_ID:-0}"; } > "$facts"

c.v: Two of those deserve their line. The working tree count turns "it worked on my machine" into a number: a report from a commit with eleven modified files is not a report about that commit. And the two empty variables,
, are there so that the day something sets them the report starts carrying them without another change; until then

parameter and one more thing to do in

c.v: Every scenario gets that line, and that is the reason for doing it here rather than in the shell. The simulated length appears in a verdict only for

c.v: Leave either of them out and nothing complains.
accepts an argument the description never declared, stores it as a launch configuration that nothing reads, and starts the run; the parameter keeps its empty default,

skips the append, and the factor comes out blank on every run. That failure looks exactly like the one the next paragraph describes, which is why it is worth knowing both: if the factor is missing, check that the launch file forwards
before you go looking in Gazebo's log for a crash that never happened.

blocks.text:
started=$(date +%s.%N)
timeout --signal=INT 180 ros2 launch bench_sim scenario.launch.py \
  scenario:="$name" verdict_file:="$verdict" facts_file:="$facts" "${@:2}" || true
wall=$(echo "$(date +%s.%N) - $started" | bc)
simulated=$(sed -n 's/^simulated seconds: //p' "$facts" | tail -1)
{ echo "[timing]"
  echo "wall seconds: $(printf '%.1f' "$wall")"
  echo "real-time factor: $([ -n "$simulated" ] && echo "scale=2; $simulated / $wall" | bc)"; } >> "$facts"
install/bench_core/bin/run_report "$name" "$facts" "$verdict" > "results/$name.md"

c.v: The factor comes out empty when the runner wrote no simulated length, which is what happens when the launch died before
ran. That case is worth getting right rather than defaulting to zero: a zero looks like a measurement and sits quietly in the table, while an empty value puts
on the report's list of what was not recorded, where somebody will see it.

The real-time factor here is the whole run's, start-up included, which is the honest number for "what did this cost" and the wrong one for "how fast does the simulation run". The scenario runner topic measured the second one over the scenario's own stretch; keep them apart and label them, because a factor of 0.6 that is mostly Gazebo starting says something different from a factor of 0.6 while the robot drives.

Give the three files a run leaves, what each is for, and which of them a person reads. Then the four questions a report has to answer without help, and the one you had to add a field for. Then the checklist in
, the six facts on it, and which two the bench cannot yet fill, with the topic that closes each.

Finish with the two real-time factors and why they are labelled apart: the one over the whole command, which is what a run costs, and the one over the scenario's own stretch, which is how fast the simulation ran. A reader who confuses them will tune the wrong thing.
